subject: Agriculture
title: India's Groundwater Crisis
description: A micro-lesson that makes India's Groundwater Crisis usable.

hook.text: India uses more groundwater than any country on Earth. Over 30 million wells pump water for farming.

buildup.text: Government subsidies provide free electricity for well pumps. Farmers have no financial reason to conserve.

discovery.text: Water tables are dropping across northern India. Wells that once hit water at 30 feet now need 300.

twist.text: When wells run dry, farmers can't afford deeper ones. Debt and crop failure drive thousands to despair.

climax.text: Satellite data shows India's groundwater depletion is among the fastest on Earth. Time is running out.

punchline.text: Free electricity. Unlimited pumping. Empty aquifers.

quiz.question: What policy contributes to India's groundwater over-pumping?
options: Free electricity subsidies for well pumps

details.summary: India extracts more groundwater than any other country, and water tables are falling fast across major agricultural states. This topic covers the scale of over-pumping, its threat to food production, and why solutions require both policy reform and technology adoption.
details.whyItMatters: India's groundwater provides 85% of its drinking water and 60% of its irrigation. The depletion rate is so severe that some regions face complete aquifer exhaustion within decades.
takeaways: India uses more groundwater than the US and China combined
Free electricity for pumping incentivizes excessive water extraction
Northwestern states like Punjab are depleting aquifers at alarming rates

faq.question: Why is India's groundwater crisis so severe?
faq.answer: India has over 20 million wells, many extracting water faster than rainfall can recharge aquifers. Free or subsidized electricity encourages over-pumping, and the shift to water-intensive crops like rice in arid states accelerates depletion.

faq.question: What solutions could address India's groundwater depletion?
faq.answer: Solutions include metering electricity for pumps, shifting to less water-intensive crops, promoting drip irrigation, managed aquifer recharge programs, community-based water management, and pricing reforms that reflect water's true scarcity.
